title: Git Garbage Collection
description: Understand what git gc does, when to run it, and how it keeps your repository healthy.

data.text: Git garbage collection (git gc) is the maintenance command that keeps your repository healthy. It compacts loose objects into pack files, prunes unreachable objects, updates reflogs, and refreshes the repository for optimal performance. Running it regularly prevents your repository from becoming slow and bloated.
git gc combines several maintenance steps into one operation. It is safe to run at any time — Git will not delete objects that are still reachable from any ref or reflog.

items: **Pack loose objects** — Consolidates loose files in objects/ into pack files
**Prune unreachable objects** — Removes objects not reachable from any ref or reflog
**Repack** — Rebuilds pack files to optimize for delta compression
**Reflog expire** — Trims reflog entries older than the configured expiry

data.title: Run and configure git gc
data.code:
# Run garbage collection manually
git gc

# Check what gc will do without actually running it
git gc --dry-run

# Run gc aggressively (more CPU, better compression)
git gc --aggressive

# Configure auto-gc threshold (default: 6700 loose objects)
git config gc.auto 10000

# Set reflog expiry (default: 90 days)
git config gc.reflogExpire 30.days

data.title: Git runs gc automatically
data.text: Git runs gc automatically when the number of loose objects exceeds gc.auto (default: 6700). You usually do not need to run it manually unless you have just done a large history rewrite or bulk import.

items: After a large rebase or filter-branch that rewrites history
After importing a large number of commits from another repository
When git count-objects shows many loose objects
Before creating an archive or deploying a bare repository

data.text: Use git count-objects -v and git fsck to monitor repository health before and after gc. A well-maintained repository has mostly packed objects and passes fsck with no errors.

data.title: Assess and verify repository health
data.code:
# Show detailed object counts
git count-objects -v

# Output shows:
# count: 1245    (loose objects)
# size: 23456    (loose objects KB)
# in-pack: 45678 (objects in pack files)
# packs: 3       (number of pack files)
# size-pack: 89012 (pack files KB)

# Verify all objects are readable and consistent
git fsck --full

# Prune only objects unreachable and older than 2 weeks
git prune --expire 2.weeks

data.title: Pruning is dangerous without backups
data.text: git prune permanently removes unreachable objects. Before running prune manually, ensure you have backups or a recent clone. Objects in reflogs are safe, but reflogs expire.

items.question: Will git gc delete my recent commits?
items.answer: No. gc only removes objects that are unreachable from any ref or reflog entry. Active branches and recent reflog entries protect all reachable objects.

items.question: Does git gc affect my working directory?
items.answer: No. git gc only manipulates the object database and refs. Your working directory files and staged changes are unaffected.

items.question: What is the difference between git gc and git prune?
items.answer: git gc is a high-level command that calls prune internally, along with repacking and reflog expiry. Use git prune directly only for advanced maintenance.

items.question: Should I commit before running git gc?
items.answer: Uncommitted changes in your working directory and index are not affected by gc. You do not need to commit first, but committing is good hygiene regardless.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: git gc keeps repositories fast by packing objects and pruning unreachable ones
Git runs gc automatically when loose objects exceed the gc.auto threshold
Run gc manually after large history rewrites or bulk imports
Use git count-objects -v and git fsck to monitor repository health
Never prune without a backup — unreachable objects are deleted permanently
